title: Press a guarded reset button through a service port
context: Machine guarding puts the controls a technician needs behind a barrier that is there to stay shut. Resetting a jammed machine, clearing a fault on a guarded conveyor or reaching a switch behind a cage are everyday maintenance jobs, and they are done by picking up something long and thin and going through the service port rather than by opening the guard. The instruction names neither a tool nor a method, so the task is whether a policy works out that the target is unreachable by hand and that one of three bars on the rack -- the only one both long enough and thin enough -- is what gets it done. Tasks on the board that extend reach name the tool in the instruction; this one does not, and none presses a control through an opening in a barrier.
setup: One fixed layout on the station bench, nothing randomised. GUARD, bolted down, centred on the midline between the arms with its front face 365 mm out from the arm mounts: a box 200 mm wide, 166 mm deep and 100 mm tall, glazed on the front, both sides and the roof with 6 mm clear polycarbonate, in a 12 mm dark-grey painted-steel frame (four corner posts, a top and bottom rail across the front, two upright mullions, and a border around the roof panel). SERVICE PORT: one 40 mm square opening in the front glazing, centred on the guard's axis, its centre 45 mm above the bench, outlined by a 10 mm steel bezel standing 8 mm proud. CONTROL PANEL, closing the back of the guard: 12 mm stainless plate with a 38 mm bore on the port's axis. RESET BUTTON: a 34 mm diameter red illuminated plunger in that bore, standing 18 mm proud of the panel, its face 130 mm behind the inner face of the front glazing and on the port's axis; spring-returned (220 N/m, 14 mm of travel), it springs back out whenever nothing holds it in. TOOL RACK, bolted down nearer the arms: six 22 mm square painted-steel posts whose tops stand 37 mm above the bench, in pairs under each of three bars, so each bar's axis lies level with the port. BARS, loose, each lying along the bench pointing away from the arms: (1) a reach rod 280 mm overall -- a 16 mm square aluminium shaft with an 80 x 28 mm handle at its near end, 55 g, gripped at that handle 40 mm from its near end, on posts 160 mm apart, centred 250 mm out and 200 mm to the left of the midline; (2) an oak rule 140 x 30 x 5 mm, 20 g, on posts 90 mm apart, centred 200 mm out and 300 mm to the left; (3) an oak baton 280 x 55 x 55 mm, 460 g, on posts 160 mm apart, centred 250 mm out and 195 mm to the right. Only the reach rod is both long enough to reach the button and thin enough to pass the port.
scoring: Measured on the best state the trial reaches. 1.0: the button held at least 5 mm in for a continuous second while a bar lies through the port -- its far end inside the guard and at least 50 mm past the guard's front face, its near end still outside it, and the bar within 12 degrees of horizontal. 0.5: any bar's end at least 50 mm inside the guard, without the button pressed. 0.25: the reach rod's centre moved at least 30 mm from where it sat on its rack. 0.0: otherwise. Full score comes only from the held press; the partial-credit scorer stops at 0.5, so a momentary touch cannot latch 1.0. Every condition is a length: in the real world, measure the button's travel against the panel face with a 5 mm feeler or a depth gauge, measure how far the bar still protrudes from the port and subtract it from the bar's known 280 mm, and check whether the rod is off its rack.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. The button springs back out by itself as soon as the bar is withdrawn; check it stands 18 mm proud again. Lay the three bars back across their posts, each along the bench, centres 250, 200 and 250 mm out from the arm mounts respectively. The guard, the control panel and the rack are bolted down and do not move.
fidelity: Rigid bodies throughout, 240 Hz PhysX, 20 Hz control. The spring is a prismatic joint with a linear force drive (220 N/m, 6 N.s/m damping) rather than a real spring: the return is perfectly linear, with no detent or stiction, and the joint constrains the button exactly to its axis instead of letting it rattle in its bore. Nothing deforms: a real reach rod cantilevered 240 mm from the grip would sag about a millimetre and flex when it met the button, and here it does not. The rod's handle is modelled as part of the same rigid body, which is also why it works: a plain bar gripped near its end droops out of the port, and the handle's mass next to the jaws is what holds it level. The guard is modelled as clean glazing in a frame, with no fasteners and no haze, and the port has sharp square edges with no chamfer, so it offers no lead-in. Friction and restitution are set per body for the real pairing: polycarbonate and the button on steel 0.40/0.33 static/dynamic with 0.25 restitution, steel on steel 0.60/0.50 with 0.45, aluminium on steel 0.55/0.45 with 0.40, oak on steel 0.40/0.32 with 0.30. Contacts start 5 mm out and rest at zero separation, as the rig's own objects do. The embodiment carries no contact sensors, so how hard the guard is hit cannot be measured and is not scored; the guard is a static collider, so a collision simply stops the arm. The layout is fixed, with no reset jitter.
